Error Propagation and Model Collapse in Diffusion Models: A Theoretical Study

Naïl B. Khelifa Affiliation: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom Correspondence to: nbk24@cam.ac.uk    Richard E. Turner Affiliation: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom Correspondence to: ret26@cam.ac.uk    Ramji Venkataramanan Affiliation: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom Correspondence to: rv285@cam.ac.uk
Abstract

Machine learning models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on synthetic data. Recursively training on such data has been observed to significantly degrade performance in a wide range of tasks, often characterized by a progressive drift away from the target distribution. In this work, we theoretically analyze this phenomenon in the setting of score-based diffusion models. For a realistic pipeline where each training round uses a combination of synthetic data and fresh samples from the target distribution, we obtain upper and lower bounds on the accumulated divergence between the generated and target distributions. This allows us to characterize different regimes of drift, depending on the score estimation error and the proportion of fresh data used in each generation. We also provide empirical results on synthetic data and images to illustrate the theory.

Keywords: 
score-based generative modeling, self-training, model collapse, stability, divergence bounds

1 Introduction

As generative AI becomes ubiquitous, synthetic data is increasingly being used for training (Zelikman et al., 2022; Gulcehre et al., 2023). However, it has been observed that performance of a model can degrade dramatically when trained predominantly on its own output (Briesch et al., 2024; Alemohammad et al., 2024a), a phenomenon often termed model collapse (Shumailov et al., 2024; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024a). For example, with recursive self-training a generative model may lose the tails of the target distribution or exhibit a marked decrease in diversity (Dohmatob et al., 2024b; Shi et al., 2025). In general, model collapse manifests as a progressive drift away from the target distribution with each training round. In this paper, we theoretically analyze this phenomenon for score-based diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020b; Song et al., 2021), which achieve state-of-the-art performance for text-to-image, text-to-audio, and video generation (Saharia et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Ho et al., 2022) as well as in a range of scientific applications (Watson et al., 2023; Corso et al., 2023).

There is a growing body of theoretical work studying the effects of recursively training machine learning models with a combination of real and synthetic data. However, this has largely been in the context of either regression models (Dohmatob et al., 2024a; Dohmatob et al., 2025; Dey et al., 2025; Vu et al., 2025; Garg et al., 2025) or maximum-likelihood type estimators for learning parametric distributions (Bertrand et al., 2024; Suresh et al., 2025; Barzilai and Shamir, 2025; Kanabar and Gastpar, 2025). Various authors have studied model collapse in diffusion and flow models empirically, and proposed techniques to mitigate it (Alemohammad et al., 2024b; Shi et al., 2025; Yoon et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025), but to our knowledge, there is still no theoretical analysis quantifying how the performance of diffusion models evolves with successive retraining.

Setting

We study a recursive training procedure in which the training data in each round is a combination of fresh samples from the true data distribution and synthetic samples generated by the current diffusion model. Let pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} denote the (unknown) true data distribution on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. We refer to each training round as a generation, and denote the model distribution at the end of generation ii by p^i\hat{p}^{i} for i≥0i\geq 0, with p^0=pdata\hat{p}^{0}=p_{\mathrm{data}}. At each generation i≥1i\geq 1, the training data consists of:

  • •

    a proportion α\alpha of fresh samples drawn from pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}, and

  • •

    a proportion (1−α)(1-\alpha) of synthetic samples drawn from the current model p^i\hat{p}^{i}.

We emphasize that the samples are not labeled as fresh or synthetic. This captures a realistic setting where the training is agnostic to how the samples were generated. Therefore, at the population level, the effective training distribution for generation i≥1i\geq 1 is the mixture

qi:=α​pdata+(1−α)​p^i.q_{i}:=\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data}}+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i}. (1)

A score network is trained on samples from qiq_{i}, which is then used to produce the next synthetic distribution p^i+1\hat{p}^{i+1}. This defines the recursion

p^i→mix with ​pdataqi→train modelp^i+1.\hat{p}^{i}\;\xrightarrow{\text{mix with }p_{\mathrm{data}}}\;q_{i}\;\xrightarrow{\text{train model}}\;\hat{p}^{i+1}. (2)

The goal of this work is to answer the following question:

In this recursive setting, how do errors accumulate over generations and how does the divergence between p^i\hat{p}^{i} and pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} evolve?

Figure 1 illustrates the effect of different mixing proportions on a recursively trained diffusion model, for pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} a 10-dimensional mixture of Gaussians. Figure 8 in Appendix G.2 shows similar behavior for the Fashion-MNIST dataset (Xiao et al., 2017), i.e., pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is the distribution that uniformly samples images from the original dataset.

Learning Target

At a high-level, training a diffusion model is equivalent to learning the score function of pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} corrupted with Gaussian noise, at a range of noise levels (Song et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023c). Although the intention is to learn pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}, the score network at generation ii is trained on samples drawn from the mixture qiq_{i}. At the population level, the identifiable target of training is therefore the score of qiq_{i}, not the score of pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}. This mismatch between the intended target and the learned target is a fundamental source of error under recursive training. Furthermore, the score network does not error learn the score of qiq_{i} perfectly (due to finite-sample and function approximation errors). This score matching error propagates through the stochastic differential equation (SDE) defining the diffusion model (the “reverse SDE” in (8)), because of which the learned distribution p^i+1\hat{p}^{i+1} will differ from qiq_{i}. Characterizing this error propagation is crucial for understanding the divergence of p^i+1\hat{p}^{i+1} from pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} as ii grows.

We track the evolution of the recursion using two quantities based on the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence (defined in (5)):

  • •

    Accumulated divergence, measuring the divergence between the ii-th generation model and the true data distribution:

    Di:=χ2(p^i∥pdata).D_{i}:=\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{data}}). (3)
  • •

    The intra-generation divergence, measuring the error introduced in one training round:

    Ii:=χ2(p^i+1∥qi).I_{i}:=\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\,\|\,q_{i}). (4)

We work primarily with the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence because, in the perturbative regime relevant for our analysis, it is equivalent to the KL divergence up to universal constants (see empirical evidence in Figure 4, where our bounds holds for both divergences), while yielding a particularly convenient algebra under the refresh step qi=α​pdata+(1−α)​p^iq_{i}=\alpha p_{\mathrm{data}}+(1-\alpha)\hat{p}^{i} that makes the cross-generation recursion explicit.

Main contributions

The recursion induced by training on real-synthetic mixtures involves two competing effects: error mitigation from the fresh data used in each step, and error accumulation from imperfect score learning and sampling. Our contributions quantify both terms and their interaction across a growing number of generations.

1. Lower bound for intra-generation divergence: We provide a lower bound (Proposition 3.3) for IiI_{i} that, for small score errors, is the product of two diffusion-specific terms: (i) observability of errors at the endpoint of the diffusion path (captured by a coefficient ηi\eta_{i}), and (ii) the energy of the path-wise score error.

χ2(p^i+1∥qi)⏟Intra-GenerationalDivergence≳ηi⏟Observabilityof Errors⋅ε⋆,i2⏟Score ErrorEnergy\underbrace{\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Intra-Generational}\\ \text{Divergence}\end{subarray}}\;\gtrsim\;\underbrace{\eta_{i}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Observability}\\ \text{of Errors}\end{subarray}}\,\cdot\,\underbrace{\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Score Error}\\ \text{Energy}\end{subarray}}

To our knowledge, this is the first lower bound for diffusion models quantifying the discrepancy between the learned distribution and the target.

2. Intra-generation Divergence Control via Score Error: Combining the above lower bound with a standard upper bound (Proposition 3.1), and proving an equivalence between the score error energies on the ideal-path and the learned-path (for small errors), we show in Theorem 3.4 that in this regime IiI_{i} is equivalent to the score error energy (up to constants): χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≍ε⋆,i2\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})\;\asymp\;\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}.

3. Long-horizon regimes and a discounted accumulation law. We analyze the accumulated divergence DND_{N} for small per-generation score errors, and identify a dichotomy as the generation NN grows (Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 4.2): (i) if the score error energies do not decay fast enough (e.g. a nonzero error floor so that ∑kε⋆,k2=+∞\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{\star,k}^{2}=+\infty), then DND_{N} cannot vanish with growing NN; (ii) if ∑kε⋆,k2<∞\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{\star,k}^{2}<\infty, then DND_{N} remains stable (uniformly bounded) with growing NN. Moreover, the accumulated divergence after a finite number of generations NN admits an interpretable geometrically-discounted decomposition up to a bias term:

χ2(p^N+1∥pdata)+Cbias≍∑k=0N(1−α)2​(N−k)⏟Forgetting(real data)⋅ε⋆,k2⏟ Accumulation(synthetic data),\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{N+1}\|\,p_{\text{data}})+C_{\textrm{bias}}\;\asymp\;\sum_{k=0}^{N}\underbrace{(1-\alpha)^{2(N-k)}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Forgetting}\\ \text{(real data)}\end{subarray}}\cdot\hskip-5.0pt\underbrace{\varepsilon_{\star,k}^{2}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{ Accumulation}\\ \text{(synthetic data)}\end{subarray}},

which shows that errors from mm generations in the past are suppressed by a factor (1−α)2​m(1-\alpha)^{2m}, quantifying the effect of α\alpha, the proportion of fresh data used in each training round. Qualitatively, this is consistent with empirical and theoretical work in a variety of settings showing that incorporating fresh data in each training round can mitigate model collapse, e.g. (Gerstgrasser et al., 2024b; Zhu et al., 2025; Bertrand et al., 2024; Dey et al., 2025).

We also provide experiments on simulated data and images to illustrate the validity of our bounds. Our results are relevant in the regime where the energy of the path-wise score error (defined in (10)) is small for all but a few generations. This regime is of interest since we seek to quantify how the intra-generation and accumulated divergences evolve when the score is estimated with high accuracy in each generation. However, we note that the number of samples for the score error to be accurately estimate may grow exponentially in the dimension dd (see (12)).

2 Background and Model Assumptions

Forward diffusion

To define the score-matching objective and the subsequent sampling procedure, we associate to each qiq_{i} a forward diffusion process on a truncated time interval [t0,T][t_{0},T], with 0<t0<T0<t_{0}<T. We consider the following variance-preserving Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (Karatzas and Shreve, 2014; Song et al., 2021):

d​𝐗ti=−12​𝐗ti​d​t+d​𝐁t,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{i}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{i}\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t}, (6)

where (𝐁t)t∈[0,T](\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} is a standard dd-dimensional Brownian motion. The process is initialized with 𝐗0i\mathbf{X}_{0}^{i} drawn from a suitable distribution qi,0q_{i,0}. Denote by qi,t:=Law⁡(𝐗ti)q_{i,t}:=\Law(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{i}) the time-tt marginal of the forward process, with population score 𝐬i⋆​(𝐱,t):=∇𝐱​log​qi,t​(𝐱)\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t):=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log q_{i,t}(\mathbf{x}).

Reverse-time generation and learning

Under standard regularity conditions (Anderson, 1982; Haussmann and Pardoux, 1986), the time reversal of (6) solves the reverse-time SDE:

d​𝐘si,⋆=[−12​𝐘si,⋆−𝐬i⋆​(𝐘si,⋆,s)]​d​s+d​𝐁¯s,\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star}=\big[-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star}-\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star},s)\big]\,\mathrm{d}s+\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}, (7)

integrated backward from s=Ts=T to s=0s=0. Here (𝐁¯s)s∈[0,T](\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s})_{s\in[0,T]} is another Brownian motion on the same probability space. If we run the reverse SDE starting from 𝐘Ti,⋆∼qi,T\mathbf{Y}_{T}^{i,\star}\sim q_{i,T}, then 𝐘0i,⋆∼qi,0\mathbf{Y}_{0}^{i,\star}\sim q_{i,0}. In practice, the score 𝐬i⋆\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star} is unknown and is approximated by a learned network 𝐬θi\mathbf{s}_{\theta_{i}} trained on samples from qiq_{i} in (1). Moreover, since the score function is often ill-behaved and challenging to estimate as t→0t\to 0 (Song and Ermon, 2020; Kim et al., 2022), as done in practice we truncate the learned process at s=t0>0s=t_{0}>0. We choose qi,0q_{i,0} such that qi,t0=qiq_{i,t_{0}}=q_{i}. Plugging the learned score 𝐬θi\mathbf{s}_{\theta_{i}} into the reverse dynamics yields the learned reverse process:

d​𝐘^si=[−12​𝐘^si−𝐬θi​(𝐘^si,s)]​d​s+d​𝐁¯s,\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s}^{i}=\big[-\tfrac{1}{2}\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s}^{i}-\mathbf{s}_{\theta_{i}}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s}^{i},s)\big]\mathrm{d}s+\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}, (8)

with initialization 𝐘^Ti∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈d)\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{T}^{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d}). The next generation model is thus denoted p^i+1:=Law⁡(𝐘^t0i)\hat{p}^{i+1}:=\Law(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{t_{0}}^{i}). Finally, denote the corresponding path laws on the path-space C⁡([t0,T],ℝd)C([t_{0},T],\mathbb{R}^{d}) by

ℙi⋆:=Law⁡((𝐘si,⋆)s∈[t0,T]),ℙ^i:=Law⁡((𝐘^si)s∈[t0,T]),\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}:=\Law\big((\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star})_{s\in[t_{0},T]}\big),\quad\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}:=\Law\big((\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s}^{i})_{s\in[t_{0},T]}\big),

so that the time-t0t_{0} marginals of the ideal and the learned reverse processes satisfy

𝐘t0i,⋆∼qi​ under ​ℙi⋆, and ​𝐘^t0i∼p^i+1​under ​ℙ^i.\displaystyle\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}\sim q_{i}\ \text{ under }\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star},\ \text{ and }\ \hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{t_{0}}^{i}\sim\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\ \text{under }\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}. (9)

With some abuse of notation, we use qi,p^i+1q_{i},\hat{p}^{i+1} to both the laws and the densities with respect to the Lebesgue measure.

Score error and energies

We define the pointwise score error

𝐞i​(𝐱,t):=𝐬θi​(𝐱,t)−𝐬i⋆​(𝐱,t),\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},t):=\mathbf{s}_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t),

and its path-wise energies

ε⋆,i2\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2} :=𝔼ℙi⋆​[∫t0T‖𝐞i​(𝐘si,⋆,s)‖22​𝑑s],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\!\left[\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star},s)\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right], (10)
ε^i2\displaystyle\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2} :=𝔼ℙ^i​[∫t0T‖𝐞i​(𝐘^si,s)‖22​𝑑s].\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}\!\left[\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s}^{i},s)\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right]. (11)

These quantities control the intra-generation divergence IiI_{i} defined in (4). We note that (10) is the score-matching loss for generation ii (Hyvärinen, 2005; Vincent, 2011; Song and Ermon, 2019; Ho et al., 2020a). At a finite sample level, for a training sample 𝒟i​∼i.i.d​qi\mathcal{D}_{i}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d}}{\sim}q_{i} of size nin_{i}, under appropriate assumptions, the minimax-optimal score estimation error satisfies (Zhang et al., 2024):

ε⋆,i2≲polylog⁡(ni)​ni−1​(1/t0)d/2.\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\;\lesssim\;\mathrm{polylog}(n_{i})\,n_{i}^{-1}\,(1/t_{0})^{d/2}. (12)

Similar bounds, relying on different assumptions, have been derived in various works (Oko et al., 2023; Dou et al., 2024; Wibisono et al., 2024). Our results are relevant in the regime where ε⋆,i2<1\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}<1. From (12), this requires a training sample of size ni∼(1/t0)d/2n_{i}\sim(1/t_{0})^{d/2}. However, when the distribution pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is supported on a low dimensional manifold (as is the case for images), under suitable assumptions we expect the optimal score estimation error to depend only on the intrinsic dimension d⋆≪dd^{\star}\ll d (Chen et al., 2023b).

Our main goal is to quantify how the score estimation error (10) propagates within and across generations. We make a few simplifying assumptions to keep the analysis tractable and reduce bookkeeping.

Model Assumptions

The proportion α\alpha of fresh samples used for training is strictly positive. We will assume pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} admits a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and the model distribution p^i\hat{p}^{i} is absolutely continuous with respect to pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}, for each generation ii. This is a standard assumption in analyses of diffusion models (Chen et al., 2023c; Benton et al., 2024). In addition to the score estimation error, there are two other sources of error in practice. One is due to the learned reverse process (8) being initialized with 𝐘Ti,⋆∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈d)\mathbf{Y}_{T}^{i,\star}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d}) rather than rather than 𝐘Ti,⋆∼qT\mathbf{Y}_{T}^{i,\star}\sim q_{T} used for the ideal process in (7). The KL divergence between qTq_{T} and 𝒩⁡(0,𝐈d)\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d}) converges to 0 exponentially fast in TT (Bakry et al., 2014), so we ignore this error. The second source of error is the discretization error when the reverse process is implemented in discrete-time. We do not quantify these errors as our main goal is to obtain lower bounds on the intra-generation and accumulated errors. Obtaining error propagation bounds taking these additional sources of error into account is a direction for future work.

3 Intra-generation divergence bounds

We now analyze the intra-generational mechanism by which score estimation error in generation ii translates into mismatch between the sampling output p^i+1\hat{p}^{\,i+1} and the training distribution qiq_{i} in (1). Our goal is to relate the one-step divergence IiI_{i} defined in (4) to the pathwise score-error energies defined by (10)-(11).

Key Technical Ideas and Girsanov Quantities

To quantify how local score errors propagate to the final samples, we use a change-of-measure argument based on Girsanov’s theorem (Girsanov, 1960; Le Gall, 2018). This is a key result in the theory of diffusion models that shows how the drift mismatch between the ideal and learned reverse-time processes (score error in our setting) controls the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the path-space measure ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i} with respect to ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}. Define the error martingale

Mti:=−∫t0t𝐞i(𝐘si,⋆,s)⋅d𝐁¯s,\displaystyle M_{t}^{i}:=-\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star},s)\cdot\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}, (13)

and its quadratic variation

⟨Mi⟩t=∫t0t‖𝐞i​(𝐘si,⋆,s)‖22​𝑑s.\displaystyle\langle M^{i}\rangle_{t}=\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star},s)\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s. (14)

We also define Zti:=Mti−12​⟨Mi⟩tZ_{t}^{i}:=M_{t}^{i}-\frac{1}{2}\langle M^{i}\rangle_{t}. Under mild and standard assumptions (A1 and A2 below), Girsanov’s theorem states that ℙ^i≪ℙi⋆\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}\ll\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star} and d​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆=exp⁡(ZTi)\tfrac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}=\exp(Z_{T}^{i}). Crucially, the likelihood ratio of the terminal marginals Ri:=p^i+1/qiR_{i}:=\hat{p}^{i+1}/q_{i} is obtained by projecting this path density onto the terminal state (Proposition B.1):

Ri​(𝐘t0i,⋆):=p^i+1​(𝐘t0i,⋆)qi​(𝐘t0i,⋆)=𝔼ℙi⋆​[eZTi|𝐘t0i,⋆].R_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}):=\frac{\hat{p}^{i+1}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})}{q_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\Big[e^{Z_{T}^{i}}\;\Big|\;\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}\Big]. (15)

This relation is central to our analysis as it translates functional score errors (captured by ZTiZ_{T}^{i}) into probabilistic drift. A key challenge in our analysis is obtain a good lower bound on the conditional expectation in (15). We begin with an upper bound that follows from a standard application of Girsanov’s theorem.

3.1 Upper Bound via Change of Measure

Assume there exists i0≥1i_{0}\geq 1 such that for all generations i≥i0i\geq i_{0}, the following conditions hold.

  1. (A1)

    Finite drift energy along learned paths.

    ε^i2:=𝔼ℙ^i​[∫t0T‖𝐞i​(𝐘^si,s)‖22​𝑑s]<∞.\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}:=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}\!\left[\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s}^{i},s)\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right]<\infty.
  2. (A2)

    Martingale property of the Girsanov density. The exponential eZTie^{Z_{T}^{i}} associated with the drift difference between (7) and (8) defines a true martingale on [t0,T][t_{0},T] so that the Girsanov change of measure holds. (A more precise version in stated in Appendix B.1.)

Assumptions A1-A2 impose no restriction on the form of the score error beyond finite quadratic energy and are standard in diffusion theory. They yield the following well-known upper bound relating sampling error to the pathwise score-estimation energy (Chen et al., 2023a; Chen et al., 2023c; Benton et al., 2024).

Proposition 3.1 (Intra-generational upper bound).

Under A1–A2, ℙ^i≪ℙi⋆\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}\ll\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star} and, by data processing inequality (marginalization to time t0t_{0}),

KL(p^i+1∥qi)≤KL(ℙ^i∥ℙi⋆)=12ε^i2.\mathrm{KL}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})\leq\mathrm{KL}(\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}\|\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star})=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}. (16)

For completeness, we give the proof in Appendix B.1.

3.2 Lower Bound Via Error Observability

The upper bound of Proposition 3.1 measures the entire path-space score error. Obtaining a divergence lower bound is more challenging as we have to to work with the marginal likelihood ratio given by (15).

First Challenge: Observability of Errors

It is possible that the path-space score error ε^i2>0\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}>0, but KL(p^i+1∥qi)=0\mathrm{KL}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})=0, i.e., a non-zero path-wise error may leave no trace at the end point t0t_{0} if it is orthogonal (in L2L^{2}) to all observables at t0t_{0}. This phenomenon is intrinsic, so we need an observability condition linking path-wise perturbations to the endpoint. We quantify the visibility of score errors at t0t_{0} through the following coefficient.

Definition 3.2 (Observability of Errors Coefficient).

Recalling the definition of MTiM_{T}^{i} in (13),

ηi:=Varℙi⋆​(𝔼⁡[MTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆])ε⋆,i2∈[0,1],\eta_{i}:=\frac{\mathrm{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\!\big(\mathbb{E}[M_{T}^{i}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}]\big)}{\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}}\;\in\;[0,1], (17)

with the convention ηi:=0\eta_{i}:=0 if ε⋆,i2=0\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}=0. The denominator in (17) equals Varℙi⋆​(MTi)\mathrm{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}(M_{T}^{i}), by Itô isometry (Le Gall, 2018).

The leading term in our divergence lower bound (Proposition 3.3) is proportional to ηi\eta_{i}. Hence the bound is informative whenever ηi>0\eta_{i}>0.

When is ηi>0\eta_{i}>0 in practice? By definition,

ηi=0⟺𝔼ℙi⋆[MTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆]=0ℙi⋆-a.s.,\eta_{i}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\!\big[M_{T}^{i}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}\big]=0\ \ \mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}\text{-a.s.},

i.e., ηi=0\eta_{i}=0 when the drift-mismatch martingale MTiM_{T}^{i} is conditionally orthogonal to all terminal observables. This cancellation is highly non-generic: in common parametric score models (e.g. neural networks with smooth activations (e.g. SiLU, GeLU)), due to random initialization and stochastic optimization noise we expect ηi>0\eta_{i}>0. The experiments discussed in Appendix G suggest that in realistic data-driven setups, ηi>0\eta_{i}>0 holds across generations; see Figure 7 (10-dimensional Gaussian Mixture) and Figure 9 (CIFAR-10 dataset). More generally, a simple and practically relevant sufficient condition is state dependence of the score perturbation function 𝐞i​(𝐱,t)\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},t): time-only (or purely path-orthogonal) perturbations can be averaged out by the conditional expectation, whereas perturbations coupled to the sample state 𝐱\mathbf{x} typically leave a detectable imprint on the endpoint. In particular, any nontrivial state-dependent affine component yields observability: if 𝐞i​(𝐱,t)=𝐰​𝐱+ξ⁡(t)\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},t)=\mathbf{w}\,\mathbf{x}+\xi(t) with 𝐰≠0\mathbf{w}\neq 0 and ξ\xi independent of 𝐱\mathbf{x}, then ηi>0\eta_{i}>0. This dichotomy is illustrated empirically in Figure 2, where state-dependent perturbations exhibit higher observability than time-only perturbations.

Second Challenge: Ratio of marginals

The ratio of marginals, given by (15), depends on an exponential functional of the score error along the path, projected to the endpoint. Thus, controlling marginals requires uniform integrability and moment bounds to prevent rare trajectories from dominating eZTie^{Z_{T}^{i}} and to relate its fluctuations to the scale ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}. This motivates the following regularity assumptions: moment bounds on the Girsanov ratio and the quadratic variation in (14).

  1. (A3)

    L1+δL^{1+\delta}-integrability of the Girsanov density. There exist δ>1\delta>1 and Cδ<∞C_{\delta}<\infty such that the Radon–Nikodym derivative d​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆=eZTi\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}=e^{Z_{T}^{i}} satisfies

    supi≥i0𝔼ℙi⋆​[eZTi​(1+δ)]≤Cδ.\sup_{i\geq i_{0}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\!\left[e^{Z_{T}^{i}(1+\delta)}\right]\leq C_{\delta}. (18)
  2. (A4)

    Quadratic Variation Moment. There exists Kγ<∞K_{\gamma}<\infty and γ>max⁡{2,4δ−1}\gamma>\max\{2,\frac{4}{\delta-1}\} with δ>1\delta>1 defined in A3 such that

    supi≥i0𝔼ℙi⋆​[⟨Mi⟩T2+γ]ε⋆,i2​(2+γ)≤Kγ.\sup_{i\geq i_{0}}\,\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[\langle M^{i}\rangle_{T}^{2+\gamma}]}{\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2(2+\gamma)}}\leq K_{\gamma}. (19)

Assumptions A3-A4 are required to hold for generations after some i0>0i_{0}>0, which allows to avoid the effect of arbitrary or bad initializations. Moreover, since the “memory” of the bad initial steps vanishes, the long-term behavior is determined by the regime where i≥i0i\geq i_{0}. Assumptions A3-A4 are stated with free parameters to retain flexibility; for concreteness, one may for instance fix (δ,γ)=(3,3)(\delta,\gamma)=(3,3).

We now state the main lower bound result.

Proposition 3.3 (Intra-generational Lower Bound).

Under Assumptions A1–A4, the following holds for generations i≥i0i\geq i_{0}. There exist constants c>0c>0 and C<∞C<\infty (depending only on ηi\eta_{i}, KγK_{\gamma}, CδC_{\delta}, and δ\delta) such that if the total score error satisfies the perturbative condition ε⋆,i2≤1\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\leq 1, then:

χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≥14⋅ηi⋅ε⋆,i2−C⋅ε⋆,i4.\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{4}\cdot\eta_{i}\cdot\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\;-\;C\cdot\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{4}. (20)

In particular, when ε⋆,i2≤min⁡{1,ηi8​C}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\leq\min\{1,\ \frac{\eta_{i}}{8C}\}, we obtain the clean lower bound: χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≥18⋅ηi⋅ε⋆,i2\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{8}\cdot\eta_{i}\cdot\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}.

The proof is given in Appendix D. The upper bounds of Propositions 3.1 and 3.3 are illustrated in Figure 3 for a 1010-dimensional Gaussian mixture, and compared with the empirically computed divergences.

3.3 Two-sided equivalence

Proposition 3.1 controls the intra-generation divergence from above in terms of the learned-path energy ε^i2\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}, whereas Proposition 3.3 provides a matching lower bound in terms of the ideal-path energy ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}, up to the observability factor ηi\eta_{i} and higher-order terms. To turn these complementary statements into a single equivalence Ii=χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≍ε⋆,i2,I_{i}=\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})\asymp\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}, the two energies ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2} (under ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}) and ε^i2\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2} (under ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}) as well as the two divergences KL\mathrm{KL} (upper bound) and χ2\chi^{2} (lower bound) need to be related. Under Assumptions A3 and A4, we show that these energies and divergences are equivalent. Combining these equivalence results with Propositions 3.1 and 3.3 yields the following two-sided control of the intra-generational divergence.

Theorem 3.4 (Two-Sided bounds for intra-generational divergence).

Under Assumptions A1- A4, the following holds for generations i≥i0i\geq i_{0}. There exist constants c>0c>0 and C<∞C<\infty (depending only on δ,Cδ,γ,Kγ\delta,C_{\delta},\gamma,K_{\gamma}) such that, when the perturbative condition ε⋆,i2≤min⁡{1,ηi8​C}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\leq\min\{1,\ \frac{\eta_{i}}{8C}\} holds, we have:

14ηiε⋆,i2−C⋅ε⋆,i4≤χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≤ 4ε⋆,i2+cε⋆,i4.\frac{1}{4}\,\eta_{i}\,\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\;-\;C\cdot\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{4}\;\leq\;\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})\;\leq\;4\,\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\;+\;c\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{4}.

In particular, for sufficiently small ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}, we have

χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≍ε⋆,i2.\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})\asymp\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}. (21)

The proof is given in Appendix E. This theorem shows that the intra-generational divergence is controlled by the pathwise score-error energy and that the two are equivalent (up to constants), up to observability and tail effects. Figure 4 indicates these bounds hold in a fully data-driven experiment for both the χ2\chi^{2} and KL divergences.

4 Error Accumulation Across Generations

Theorem 3.4 shows that when the score error is observable (i.e., ηi>0\eta_{i}>0), the intra-generational divergence satisfies Ii=χ2(p^i+1∥qi)I_{i}=\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i}) is equivalent (up to constants) to ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2} in the perturbative regime. We now study how this divergence propagates through the recursion (2) over many generations, recalling our assumption that the refresh rate α>0\alpha>0.

A key observation is that the fresh samples introduced in each generation contracts the accumulated divergence. Indeed, a simple calculation (Lemma F.1) shows that χ2(p^i∥pdata)=(1−α)2χ2(p^i∥pdata)\chi^{2}(\hat{p}_{i}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{data}})\;=\;(1-\alpha)^{2}\,\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{data}}). In contrast, the score error in the next round of training increases the accumulated divergence. These two competing effects determine the evolution of Di=χ2(qi∥pdata)D_{i}=\chi^{2}(q_{i}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{data}}) as ii grows. We distinguish two cases, assuming small score errors in each generation: if ∑i≥0ε⋆,i2=∞\sum_{i\geq 0}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}=\infty, then we show that DiD_{i} and cannot converge to 00. On the other hand, if ∑i≥0ε⋆,i2<∞\sum_{i\geq 0}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}<\infty, we show that (up to constants) DiD_{i} is given by a discounted sum of score error energies from past generations.

4.1 Persistent Errors

Proposition 4.1 (Persistent Errors).

Assume A1-A4, and that for i≥i0i\geq i_{0}, ηi≥η¯>0\eta_{i}\geq\underline{\eta}>0 and ε⋆,i2≤min⁡{1,ηi8​C}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\leq\min\{1,\ \frac{\eta_{i}}{8C}\}. Then:

(i) Non-summable score error implies non-summable global drift. If ∑i≥0ε⋆,i2=+∞\sum_{i\geq 0}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}=+\infty, then ∑i≥0Di=+∞\sum_{i\geq 0}D_{i}=+\infty and (Di)i≥0(D_{i})_{i\geq 0} cannot converge to 00.

(ii) A score-error floor implies persistent accumulated divergence. If ε⋆,i2≥ε¯>0\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\geq\underline{\varepsilon}>0 for all sufficiently large ii, then

lim supi→∞Di≥α16​(1+(1−α)2)⋅η¯​ε¯,\limsup_{i\to\infty}D_{i}\geq\frac{\alpha}{16(1+(1-\alpha)^{2})}\cdot\underline{\eta}\,\underline{\varepsilon},

In particular, the sequence (Di)(D_{i}) exhibits infinitely many macroscopic deviations from pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}.

4.2 Controlled Errors

We now bound the accumulated divergence DiD_{i} when the score errors ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2} are summable, under a technical assumption defined in terms of an adaptive tail set.

An adaptive tail assumption

For a constant ζi∈(0,1)\zeta_{i}\in(0,1), define the adaptive “good” set

𝒢i:={𝐱:|p^i​(𝐱)/pdata​(𝐱)−1|≤Di/ζi}.\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{i}:=\{\mathbf{x}:\left|\hat{p}^{\,i}(\mathbf{x})/p_{\mathrm{data}}(\mathbf{x})-1\right|\leq\sqrt{D_{i}/\zeta_{i}}\}. (22)

Since 𝔼pdata​[|p^i​(x)/pdata− 1|2]=Di\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}[|\hat{p}^{\,i}(x)/p_{\mathrm{data}}\,-\,1|^{2}]=D_{i}, Chebyshev’s inequality implies pdata​(𝒢ic)≤ζip_{\mathrm{data}}(\mathcal{G}_{i}^{c})\leq\zeta_{i}. As DiD_{i} grows, the set 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} expands and 𝒢ic\mathcal{G}_{i}^{c} consists of the regions where where p^i/pdata\hat{p}^{i}/p_{\mathrm{data}} is increasingly atypical. We then assume that the training distribution qiq_{i} does not over-emphasize this tail region in the following sense.

  1. (A5)

    There exist a generation i0≥0i_{0}\geq 0 such that, for the δ\delta in Assumption A3 and p′:=δ+1δ−1p^{\prime}:=\frac{\delta+1}{\delta-1}, there exists a constant Cζ>0C_{\zeta}>0 such that,

    supi≥i0{ζi−1​𝔼qi​[(qipdata)p′​𝟏𝒢ic]}≤Cζ.\sup_{i\geq i_{0}}\Big\{\zeta_{i}^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{q_{i}}\!\big[\Big(\frac{q_{i}}{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\Big)^{p^{\prime}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{G}_{i}^{c}}\big]\Big\}\leq C_{\zeta}.

From the definition of qiq_{i} in (1), we know that qi/pdata=α+(1−α)​p^i/pdataq_{i}/p_{\mathrm{data}}=\alpha+(1-\alpha)\hat{p}^{\,i}/p_{\mathrm{data}}, which can blow up on 𝒢ic\mathcal{G}_{i}^{c} only if p^i/pdata\hat{p}^{\,i}/p_{\mathrm{data}} is large there. Therefore, (A5) is a local condition on a vanishing tail set, which rules out spurious heavy tails that may cause the synthetic model to place large mass in regions where where pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is tiny.

Theorem 4.2 (Discounted accumulation of errors).

Assume A1-A5, and that i≥i0i\geq i_{0}, we have ηi≥η¯>0\eta_{i}\geq\underline{\eta}>0 and ε⋆,i2≤min⁡{1,ηi8​C}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\leq\min\Big\{1,\ \frac{\eta_{i}}{8C}\Big\}. Also assume that

∑i=0∞ε⋆,i2<∞.\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}<\infty.

Then, there exists a constant CbiasC_{\mathrm{bias}} defined in Equation (112) such that for each generation N≥i0N\geq i_{0},

DN+1+Cbias≍∑i=i0N(1−α)2​(N−i)​ε⋆,i2+(1−α)2​(N+1−i0)​Di0.D_{N+1}+C_{\mathrm{bias}}\asymp\sum_{i=i_{0}}^{N}(1-\alpha)^{2(N-i)}\,\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}+(1-\alpha)^{2(N+1-i_{0})}D_{i_{0}}. (23)

The proof is given in Appendix F.3, where we derive upper and lower bounds for DN+1D_{N+1} with explicit constants. Theorem 4.2 shows that in the regime where the score errors are small and summable, the accummulated divergence is a geometrically-discounted sum of square errors. In particular, errors from mm generations in the past are suppressed by a factor (1−α)2​m(1-\alpha)^{2m}, and the larger the proportion of fresh training samples in each round, the higher the rate of “forgetting” score errors. Qualitatively, this is consistent with the findings in many different settings that incorporating fresh data in each training round can mitigate model collapse (Gerstgrasser et al., 2024b; Zhu et al., 2025; Bertrand et al., 2024; Dey et al., 2025).

Figure 5 illustrates the decomposition of Theorem 4.2 for a 1010-dimensional Gaussian mixture, tracking the contribution to DN+1D_{N+1} of each term in the sum in (23). Figure 10 in Appendix G.3 shows the same behavior on the Fashion-MNIST dataset (Xiao et al., 2017)). Figure 6 in Appendix G.1 illustrates that the functional dependence predicted by Theorem 4.2 accurately captures the observed growth across generations in the 10-dimensional Gaussian mixture setting.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

We analyzed recursive training of diffusion models with a fixed proportion α>0\alpha>0 of fresh data in each training round. We derived lower and upper bounds on the intra-generation and accumulated divergences, in terms of the path-wise energy of the score error in each generation. An essential component of our lower bound is the observability coefficient in (17), which quantifies the fraction of the path-wise error energy that manifests in the learned distribution. The paper focuses on the setting where the score error energy in each generation is small. An important direction for future work is to establish bounds in the large error regime. Obtaining a lower bound in this regime, even for one generation, is challenging because the ratio between the learned and ideal densities (given by the projection of the path-wise ratio in (15)) cannot be linearized with reasonable control of the remainder term. Another direction for further work is to taking into account the discretization error due to the diffusion being implemented in discrete-time. Finally, a key open question is: is there is a limiting distribution to which the model converges when recursively trained, and if so, how does it depend on α\alpha and pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}?

Appendix A Preliminaries and notation for Appendices

We consider reverse-time diffusions on the interval [t0,T][t_{0},T] (integrated from TT down to t0t_{0}). Let 𝐁¯=(𝐁¯s)s∈[t0,T]\bar{\mathbf{B}}=(\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s})_{s\in[t_{0},T]} denote a standard Brownian motion in reverse time on a filtered space (Ω,ℱ,(ℱs)s∈[t0,T])(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_{s})_{s\in[t_{0},T]}).

Indexing. The superscript ii denotes the generation (self-training iteration). Within each generation we compare: (i) an ideal reverse process (driven by the exact score) and (ii) a learned reverse process (driven by the estimated score).

Reverse-time SDEs and path measures. For s∈[t0,T]s\in[t_{0},T], the ideal and learned reverse-time processes solve

d​𝐘si,⋆=[−12​𝐘si,⋆−𝐬i⋆​(𝐘si,⋆,s)]​d​s+d​𝐁¯s,d​𝐘^si=[−12​𝐘^si−𝐬θi​(𝐘^si,s)]​d​s+d​𝐁¯s,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}_{s}=\Big[-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}_{s}-\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star}(\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}_{s},s)\Big]\mathrm{d}s+\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s},\qquad\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}_{s}=\Big[-\tfrac{1}{2}\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}_{s}-\mathbf{s}_{\theta_{i}}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}_{s},s)\Big]\mathrm{d}s+\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s},

with independent initializations 𝐘Ti,⋆,𝐘^Ti∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}_{T},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). We write ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star} (resp. ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}) for the law on path space C⁡([t0,T],ℝd)C([t_{0},T],\mathbb{R}^{d}) induced by 𝐘i,⋆\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star} (resp. 𝐘^i\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}).

Score error and energy. The score (drift) discrepancy is

𝐞i​(𝐱,t):=𝐬θi​(𝐱,t)−𝐬i⋆​(𝐱,t),\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},t):=\mathbf{s}_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t),

and we use the shorthand 𝐞i​(s):=𝐞i​(𝐘si,⋆,s)\mathbf{e}_{i}(s):=\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}_{s},s) or 𝐞i​(𝐘^si,s)\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}_{s},s) depending on the ambient measure. We distinguish two integrated error energies:

ε⋆,i2:=𝔼ℙi⋆​[∫t0T‖𝐞i​(𝐘si,⋆,s)‖2​𝑑s],ε^i2:=𝔼ℙ^i​[∫t0T‖𝐞i​(𝐘^si,s)‖22​𝑑s].\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\!\left[\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}_{s},s)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right],\qquad\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}:=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}\!\left[\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}_{s},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right].

Ri​(𝐱):=p^i+1​(𝐱)qi​(𝐱),Ti​(𝐱):=qi​(𝐱)pdata​(𝐱), where ​qi:=α​pdata+(1−α)​p^i.R_{i}(\mathbf{x}):=\frac{\hat{p}^{\,i+1}(\mathbf{x})}{q_{i}(\mathbf{x})},\qquad T_{i}(\mathbf{x}):=\frac{q_{i}(\mathbf{x})}{p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})},\qquad\text{ where }q_{i}:=\alpha p_{\mathrm{data}}+(1-\alpha)\hat{p}^{\,i}.

Appendix B Intra-generational likelihood ratios via Girsanov’s theorem

B.1 Proof of Upper Bound (Proposition 3.1)

We recall the definitions of the ideal and learned reverse-time processes on s∈[t0,T]s\in[t_{0},T] (integrated backward from TT to t0t_{0}) from (7) and (8), with independent initializations 𝐘Ti,⋆,𝐘^Ti∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}_{T},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\,i}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). Recall we defined two path-space probability measures ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star} and ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i} on the path space C⁡([t0,T],ℝd)C([t_{0},T],\mathbb{R}^{d}):

  • •

    ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}: The law of the ideal reverse-time process 𝐘i,⋆\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star}. It is initialized at end time TT with Gaussian noise, and its dynamics are driven by the exact score 𝐬i⋆\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star}. Its terminal marginal at t0t_{0} is the current mixing distribution qiq_{i}.

  • •

    ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}: The law of the learned reverse-time process 𝐘^i\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{i}. It is initialized at TT with Gaussian noise, and its dynamics are driven by the approximate score 𝐬θi\mathbf{s}_{\theta_{i}}. Its terminal marginal at t0t_{0} is the next-generation distribution p^i+1\hat{p}^{i+1}.

The drift discrepancy is given by the score error: 𝐞i​(𝐱,t):=𝐬^θi​(𝐱,t)−𝐬i⋆​(𝐱,t)\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},t):=\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t). Recall that we operate under the following assumptions:

  • A1

    Finite drift energy. The learned path measure satisfies 𝔼ℙ^i​[∫t0T‖𝐞i​(𝐘^s,s)‖22​𝑑s]<∞\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}[\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s]<\infty.

  • A2

    Martingale property. From (13)-(14) recall that for s∈[t0,T]s\in[t_{0},T],

    Msi:=−∫t0s𝐞i(𝐘ui,⋆,u)⋅d𝐁¯u,⟨Mi⟩s:=∫t0s∥𝐞i(𝐘ui,⋆,u)∥22du,Zsi=Msi−12⟨Mi⟩s.M_{s}^{i}:=-\int_{t_{0}}^{s}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{u}^{i,\star},u)\cdot\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{u},\qquad\langle M^{i}\rangle_{s}:=\int_{t_{0}}^{s}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{u}^{i,\star},u)\|^{2}_{2}\mathrm{d}u,\qquad Z_{s}^{i}=M_{s}^{i}-\frac{1}{2}\langle M^{i}\rangle_{s}.

    Define the Doléans–Dade exponential

    Us:=exp⁡(Msi−12​⟨Mi⟩s).U_{s}:=\exp\left(M_{s}^{i}-\frac{1}{2}\langle M^{i}\rangle_{s}\right).

    We assume (Us)s∈[t0,T](U_{s})_{s\in[t_{0},T]} defines a true ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}^{\star}_{i}-martingale on [t0,T][t_{0},T].

Discussion on Assumptions A1 and A2.

These assumptions ensures that the Girsanov transformation yields a valid probability measure (i.e., 𝔼ℙi⋆​[UT]=1\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[U_{T}]=1). While UsU_{s} is guaranteed to be a local martingale by construction, different sufficient conditions can be found in the literature to guarantee the full martingale status. The most common ones are:

  • •

    Novikov’s condition (Novikov, 1973):

    𝔼ℙi⋆​[exp⁡(12​∫t0T‖𝐞i​(𝐘si,⋆,s)‖22​𝑑s)]<∞.\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\left[\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right)\right]<\infty.
  • •

    Beneš Condition (Beneš, 1971): the drift discrepancy satisfies a linear growth bound

    ‖𝐞i​(𝐱,t)‖2≤C⁡(1+‖𝐱‖2),C>0.\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},t)\|_{2}\leq C(1+\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}),\qquad C>0.

    In the context of diffusion models parameterized by neural networks, this holds if the network weights are finite and the activation functions are Lipschitz (e.g., ReLU, SiLU) or bounded (e.g., Tanh, Sigmoid), provided the domain is effectively bounded or the growth is controlled.

  • •

    Stopping Time Condition. Finally, another popular assumption relies on stopping times. Formally, the exponential process (Us)s∈[t0,T](U_{s})_{s\in[t_{0},T]} is always a local martingale. This implies the existence of a non-decreasing sequence of stopping times {τn}n≥1\{\tau_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} such that τn↑T\tau_{n}\uparrow T almost surely as n→∞n\to\infty, and for every nn, the stopped process (Us∧τn)s∈[t0,T](U_{s\wedge\tau_{n}})_{s\in[t_{0},T]} is a true martingale. A canonical choice for these stopping times is defined by the accumulation of the drift energy:

    τn:=inf{s∈[t0,T]:∫t0s‖𝐞i​(𝐘ui,⋆,u)‖22​𝑑u≥n}∧T.\tau_{n}:=\inf\left\{s\in[t_{0},T]:\int_{t_{0}}^{s}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{u}^{i,\star},u)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}u\geq n\right\}\wedge T. (24)

    By definition, the accumulated energy up to time τn\tau_{n} is bounded by nn. Consequently, the conditional Novikov criterion is trivially satisfied for the stopped process:

    𝔼⁡[exp⁡(12​∫t0τn‖𝐞i​(𝐘si,⋆,s)‖22​𝑑u)]≤en/2<∞.\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\int_{t_{0}}^{\tau_{n}}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{i,\star},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)\right]\leq e^{n/2}<\infty.

    This guarantees that 𝔼⁡[Uτn]=1\mathbb{E}[U_{\tau_{n}}]=1 for all nn. Assumption A2 is therefore equivalent to the condition that the sequence is uniformly integrable, allowing the equality to hold in the limit: 𝔼⁡[UT]=limn→∞𝔼⁡[Uτn]=1\mathbb{E}[U_{T}]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[U_{\tau_{n}}]=1. This stopping time condition has been used in previous analyses of the convergence properties of diffusion models (Chen et al., 2023c; Benton et al., 2024).

Proof of Proposition 3.1.

Step 1: Pathwise Change of Measure via Girsanov. The ideal process 𝐘i,⋆\mathbf{Y}^{i,\star} and learned process 𝐘^i\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{i} are defined on the filtered probability space (Ω,ℱ,(ℱs)s∈[t0,T],ℙi⋆)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_{s})_{s\in[t_{0},T]},\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}) equipped with the standard Brownian motion 𝐁¯\bar{\mathbf{B}}. They share the same diffusion coefficient (the identity matrix) and differ only in their drift terms. Specifically, the drift difference is Δ​𝐛​(𝐱,s)=−𝐞i​(𝐱,s)\Delta\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x},s)=-\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},s).

To relate their laws, we employ Girsanov’s theorem (Cameron and Martin, 1944; Girsanov, 1960; Le Gall, 2018). The candidate density process is the stochastic exponential (Doléans-Dade exponential (Doléans-Dade, 1970)) of MiM^{i},

Us=exp⁡(Msi−12​⟨Mi⟩s).U_{s}=\exp\left(M_{s}^{i}-\frac{1}{2}\langle M^{i}\rangle_{s}\right).

By Itô’s formula (Karatzas and Shreve, 2014; Le Gall, 2018), UsU_{s} is a nonnegative local martingale under ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star} and hence a supermartingale. By Assumption A2, (Us)s∈[t0,T](U_{s})_{s\in[t_{0},T]} is in fact a (uniformly integrable) martingale, so in particular 𝔼ℙi⋆​[UT]=Ut0=1\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[U_{T}]=U_{t_{0}}=1. Therefore, we can define the probability measure ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i} by the Radon-Nikodym derivative:

d​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆((𝐘s⋆,i)s∈[t0,T])=UT=exp(−∫t0T𝐞i(𝐘s⋆,i,s)⋅d𝐁¯s−12∫t0T∥𝐞i(𝐘s⋆,i,s)∥22ds).\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}((\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{\star,i})_{s\in[t_{0},T]})=U_{T}=\exp\left(-\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{\star,i},s)\cdot\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{\star,i},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right).

Under this new measure ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}, the process 𝐁^s:=𝐁¯s+∫t0s𝐞i​(𝐘u,u)​𝑑u\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{s}:=\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}+\int_{t_{0}}^{s}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{u},u)\mathrm{d}u is a standard Brownian motion (by the Girsanov theorem), and the coordinate process 𝐘\mathbf{Y} satisfies the SDE of the learned diffusion 𝐘^i\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{i}. Thus, ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i} is precisely the law of the learned process.

Step 2: KL Divergence Calculation. The Kullback-Leibler divergence is defined as KL(ℙ^i∥ℙi⋆)=𝔼ℙ^i[logd​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆]\mathrm{KL}(\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}\|\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star})=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}]. We express the log-density ratio in terms of the process 𝐘^\hat{\mathbf{Y}} (governed by ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}). Under ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}, we can write d​𝐁¯s=d​𝐁^s−𝐞i​(𝐘^s,s)​d​s\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}=\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{s}-\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\mathrm{d}s, where 𝐁^\hat{\mathbf{B}} is a standard Brownian motion under ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}. Substituting this into the log-likelihood ratio:

log⁡d​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆​((𝐘^s)s∈[t0,T])\displaystyle\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}((\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s})_{s\in[t_{0},T]}) =−∫t0T𝐞i(𝐘^s,s)⋅d𝐁¯s−12∫t0T∥𝐞i(𝐘^s,s)∥22ds\displaystyle=-\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\cdot\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s
=−∫t0T𝐞i⋅(d𝐁^s−𝐞ids)−12∫t0T∥𝐞i(𝐘^s,s)∥22ds\displaystyle=-\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbf{e}_{i}\cdot(\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{s}-\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathrm{d}s)-\frac{1}{2}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s
=−∫t0T𝐞i(𝐘^s,s)⋅d𝐁^s+12∫t0T∥𝐞i(𝐘^s,s)∥22ds.\displaystyle=-\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\cdot\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{s}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s.

Taking expectation under ℙ^i\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}:

𝔼ℙ^i[logd​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆]=𝔼ℙ^i[−∫t0T𝐞i⋅d𝐁^s]+12𝔼ℙ^i[∫t0T∥𝐞i(𝐘^s,s)∥22ds].\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}\left[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}\left[-\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbf{e}_{i}\cdot\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{s}\right]+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}\left[\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\|\mathbf{e}_{i}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{s},s)\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right].

The first term is the expectation of a stochastic integral. Under Assumption A1, the integrand is square-integrable, so the stochastic integral is a true martingale starting at 0, and its expectation vanishes. The second term is exactly 12​ε^i2\frac{1}{2}\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}.

Step 3: Marginalization (Data Processing). Let πt0:C⁡([t0,T])→ℝd\pi_{t_{0}}:C([t_{0},T])\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be the projection map ω↦ω⁡(t0)\omega\mapsto\omega(t_{0}). The marginal distributions are push-forwards: p^i+1=(πt0)#​ℙ^i\hat{p}^{i+1}=(\pi_{t_{0}})_{\#}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i} and qi=(πt0)#​ℙi⋆q_{i}=(\pi_{t_{0}})_{\#}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}. By the data processing inequality (contraction of KL under push-forward):

KL(p^i+1∥qi)≤KL(ℙ^i∥ℙi⋆)=12ε^i2.\mathrm{KL}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i})\leq\mathrm{KL}(\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}\|\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star})=\frac{1}{2}\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}.

∎

B.2 Relating Marginals via Girsanov’s Theorem

Proposition B.1 (Marginal Ratio Representation).

Under Assumptions A1 and A2, the Radon-Nikodym derivative between the path measures is given by eZTie^{Z_{T}^{i}}, where ZTi=MTi−12​⟨Mi⟩TZ_{T}^{i}=M_{T}^{i}-\frac{1}{2}\langle M^{i}\rangle_{T}. Consequently, the marginal likelihood ratio satisfies:

Proof.

As shown in Appendix B.1, we have d​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆=exp⁡(ZTi)\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\;=\;\exp\left(Z_{T}^{i}\right). Next, we restrict this relation to the marginals at time t0t_{0}. Let f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be any bounded measurable test function acting on the data space. We compute the expectation of ff under the generated distribution p^i+1\hat{p}^{i+1}:

𝔼𝐱∼p^i+1​[f​(𝐱)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\hat{p}^{i+1}}[f(\mathbf{x})] =𝔼ℙ^i​[f⁡(𝐘^t0i)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}[f(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{t_{0}}^{i})] (Definition of marginal)
=𝔼ℙi⋆​[f⁡(𝐘t0i,⋆)​d​ℙ^id​ℙi⋆]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\left[f(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\right] (Change of measure)
=𝔼ℙi⋆​[f⁡(𝐘t0i,⋆)​eZTi]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\left[f(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})\,e^{Z_{T}^{i}}\right] (Definition of ​ZTi​)\displaystyle\text{(Definition of }Z_{T}^{i}\text{)}
=𝔼ℙi⋆​[f⁡(𝐘t0i,⋆)​𝔼ℙi⋆​[eZTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\left[f(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[e^{Z_{T}^{i}}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}]\right] (Tower property).\displaystyle\text{(Tower property)}.

Comparing the first and last lines, we identify 𝔼ℙi⋆​[eZTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆]\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[e^{Z_{T}^{i}}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}] as the density ratio p^i+1qi\frac{\hat{p}^{i+1}}{q_{i}}. ∎

Appendix D Proof of The Intra-Generational Lower Bound (Proposition 3.3)

From Proposition B.1, recall that the ratio p^i+1qi\frac{\hat{p}^{i+1}}{q_{i}} is given by

Ri​(𝐘t0i,⋆):=p^i+1​(𝐘t0i,⋆)qi​(𝐘t0i,⋆)=𝔼ℙi⋆​[eZTi|𝐘t0i,⋆],qi​-almost everywhere.R_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})\;:=\;\frac{\hat{p}^{i+1}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})}{q_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\Big[e^{Z_{T}^{i}}\;\Big|\;\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}\Big],\quad q_{i}\text{-almost everywhere.}

To obtain a lower bound, we write eZTi=1+ZTi+ψ⁡(ZTi)e^{Z_{T}^{i}}=1+Z_{T}^{i}+\psi(Z_{T}^{i}) and control the remainder term ψ⁡(ZTi)\psi(Z_{T}^{i}) under the assumptions of the proposition. To this end, we will use two lemmas proved in Appendix C. The first, Lemma C.1 controls the second moment of 𝔼ℙi⋆​[ZTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆]\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\Big[Z_{T}^{i}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}\Big]. We will prove the following version of Proposition 3.3 with explicit constants.

Proposition D.1 (Intra-generational lower bound with explicit constants).

Assume A1–A4, with associated parameters (γ,Kγ)(\gamma,K_{\gamma}) and (δ,Cδ)(\delta,C_{\delta}). Let CBDG​(r)C_{\mathrm{BDG}}(r) denote a Burkholder–Davis–Gundy (Burkholder et al., 1972; Revuz and Yor, 1999) constant such that for any continuous martingale MM,

Then, for every generation i≥i0i\geq i_{0} satisfying the perturbative condition ε⋆,i2≤1\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\leq 1, one has

χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≥14ηiε⋆,i2−Cε⋆,i4,\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{4}\,\eta_{i}\,\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\;-\;C\,\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{4}, (35)

with the explicit choices

C:=Kγ22+γ8+CZ​44+14​(CBDG​(4​p′)​Kγ2​p′2+γ)1/p′​Cδ1/p,C:=\frac{K_{\gamma}^{\frac{2}{2+\gamma}}}{8}\;+\;\frac{C_{Z4}}{4}\;+\;\frac{1}{4}\,\Big(C_{\mathrm{BDG}}(4p^{\prime})\,K_{\gamma}^{\frac{2p^{\prime}}{2+\gamma}}\Big)^{\!1/p^{\prime}}\,C_{\delta}^{1/p}, (36)

κi:=min⁡{1,ηi8​C},\kappa_{i}:=\min\Big\{1,\ \frac{\eta_{i}}{8C}\Big\}, (37)

whenever ε⋆,i2≤κi\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}\leq\kappa_{i} we obtain the clean lower bound

χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≥c2ηiε⋆,i2=18ηiε⋆,i2.\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{\,i+1}\|q_{i})\;\geq\;\frac{c}{2}\,\eta_{i}\,\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}=\frac{1}{8}\,\eta_{i}\,\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}. (38)
Proof.

The proof proceeds in six steps: we expand the density ratio using Taylor’s theorem, apply Young’s inequality to isolate the leading-order term, invoke the observability lemma for the signal, control the remainder using exponential integrability, and combine all bounds.

1. Exponential expansion with controlled remainder.

Define the remainder function ψ:ℝ→ℝ\psi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} by

ψ⁡(z):=ez−1−z=∑k=2∞zkk!.\psi(z):=e^{z}-1-z=\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{z^{k}}{k!}. (39)

From Proposition B.1 (Marginal Ratio Representation), we have

Ri​(𝐘t0i,⋆)=p^i+1​(𝐘t0i,⋆)qi​(𝐘t0i,⋆)=𝔼ℙi⋆​[eZTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆].R_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})=\frac{\hat{p}^{i+1}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})}{q_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star})}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}\bigl[e^{Z_{T}^{i}}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}\bigr]. (40)

Applying the decomposition eZTi=1+ZTi+ψ⁡(ZTi)e^{Z_{T}^{i}}=1+Z_{T}^{i}+\psi(Z_{T}^{i}) and taking conditional expectations:

Ri−1\displaystyle R_{i}-1 =𝔼ℙi⋆​[eZTi−1∣𝐘t0i,⋆]=𝔼ℙi⋆​[ZTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆]+𝔼ℙi⋆​[ψ⁡(ZTi)∣𝐘t0i,⋆].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[e^{Z_{T}^{i}}-1\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[Z_{T}^{i}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[\psi(Z_{T}^{i})\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}].

We introduce the notation:

Z¯i\displaystyle\bar{Z}_{i} :=𝔼ℙi⋆[ZTi∣𝐘t0i,⋆](conditional mean of log-likelihood ratio),\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[Z_{T}^{i}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}]\quad\text{(conditional mean of log-likelihood ratio)}, (41)
Ψi\displaystyle\Psi_{i} :=𝔼ℙi⋆[ψ(ZTi)∣𝐘t0i,⋆](conditional mean of remainder).\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}}[\psi(Z_{T}^{i})\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}]\quad\text{(conditional mean of remainder)}. (42)

Thus we have the fundamental decomposition:

Ri−1=Z¯i+Ψi.R_{i}-1=\bar{Z}_{i}+\Psi_{i}. (43)

2. Quadratic lower bound via Young’s inequality.

For any ν∈(0,1)\nu\in(0,1), we apply the weighted Young’s inequality in the form (a+b)2≥(1−ν)​a2−(1ν−1)​b2(a+b)^{2}\geq(1-\nu)a^{2}-(\frac{1}{\nu}-1)b^{2}:

(Ri−1)2=(Z¯i+Ψi)2≥(1−ν)​Z¯i2−(1ν−1)​Ψi2.(R_{i}-1)^{2}=(\bar{Z}_{i}+\Psi_{i})^{2}\geq(1-\nu)\bar{Z}_{i}^{2}-\left(\frac{1}{\nu}-1\right)\Psi_{i}^{2}. (44)

Taking expectations with respect to qiq_{i} (equivalently, with respect to 𝐘t0i,⋆\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star} under ℙi⋆\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\star}):

χ2(p^i+1∥qi)=𝔼qi[(Ri−1)2]≥(1−ν)𝔼qi​[Z¯i2]⏟Signal−(1ν−1)𝔼qi​[Ψi2]⏟Remainder.\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i})=\mathbb{E}_{q_{i}}[(R_{i}-1)^{2}]\geq(1-\nu)\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{i}}[\bar{Z}_{i}^{2}]}_{\mathrm{Signal}}-\left(\frac{1}{\nu}-1\right)\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{i}}[\Psi_{i}^{2}]}_{\mathrm{Remainder}}. (45)

Remark D.2 (Optimality of Constants).

The constants c=14c=\frac{1}{4} and the specific form of CC arise from choosing ν=θ=12\nu=\theta=\frac{1}{2}. These can be optimized by choosing ν\nu and θ\theta as functions of the ratio ηi/Kγ\eta_{i}/K_{\gamma}, but the qualitative scaling χ2≳ηi​ε⋆,i2\chi^{2}\gtrsim\eta_{i}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2} is sharp.

Appendix G Experimental Validation

We validate our theoretical framework by implementing the recursive training described in Section 1 on three different datasets: a 10-dimensional Gaussian mixture model (GMM), where ground-truth quantities can be computed analytically or estimated with high precision, and for score networks trained on image datasets (Fashion-MNIST (Xiao et al., 2017) and CIFAR-10 ((Krizhevsky, 2009)). We verify both the intra-generational bounds (Propositions 3.1 and 3.3) and the global accumulation formula (Theorem 4.2) on these settings.

G.1 First Experimental Setup: 10-dimensional Gaussian Mixture

Ground-truth distribution.

We consider a mixture of five isotropic Gaussians in ℝ10\mathbb{R}^{10}:

pdata​(𝐱)=15​∑k=15𝒩⁡(𝐱,𝝁k,σ2​𝐈10),p_{\mathrm{data}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{k=1}^{5}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k},\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}_{10}), (121)

where the means {𝝁k}k=15\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{5} are placed at the origin (0,0)(0,0) and at ((−4,−4),(−4,4),(4,−4),(4,4))((-4,-4),(-4,4),(4,-4),(4,4)) and σ=0.6\sigma=0.6. This configuration creates a well-separated mixture with analytically tractable score functions.

Exact Gaussian closure for GMM data.

Contrary to realistic data distributions (e.g. images), the Gaussian initialisation for pdatap_{\text{data}} in this experiment is motivated by the close-form expressions it yields:

  • •

    Explicit score expression. The true score of pdatap_{\text{data}} can be written explicitly as:

    ∇𝐱​log​pdata​(𝐱)=∑k=15(𝒩⁡(𝐱,𝝁k,σ2​𝐈10)∑j=15𝒩⁡(𝐱,𝝁j,σ2​𝐈10))⏟Posterior probability ​πk​(𝐱)​(−𝐱−𝝁kσ2)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{k=1}^{5}\underbrace{\left(\frac{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k},\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}_{10})}{\sum_{j=1}^{5}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{j},\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}_{10})}\right)}_{\text{Posterior probability }\pi_{k}(\mathbf{x})}\left(-\frac{\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}}{\sigma^{2}}\right) (122)
  • •

    Marginals explicit expression. Because the forward diffusion is linear with additive Gaussian noise, each mixture component remains Gaussian at every diffusion time, and all time marginals are therefore Gaussian mixtures with explicitly known parameters. Moreover, both the ideal and learned reverse-time SDEs preserve Gaussianity at the component level. Consequently, for every generation ii, the generated distribution p^i\hat{p}^{\,i} and the training mixture qi=α​pdata+(1−α)​p^iq_{i}=\alpha p_{\text{data}}+(1-\alpha)\hat{p}^{\,i} are exactly Gaussian mixtures. This yields closed-form expressions for the score, drift mismatch, and quadratic variation, ensuring that all theoretical quantities appearing in the bounds are well-defined and can be evaluated with high numerical precision.

Score estimation via kernel density.

For the Gaussian mixture, rather than training neural networks, we use soft kernel density estimators (KDE) (Silverman, 1986) with bandwidth h=σ=0.6h=\sigma=0.6 to approximate the score function from samples. Given NN training samples {xj}j=1N\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}, the estimated score at diffusion time tt is:

𝐬^t​(𝐱)=∑j=1Nwj​(𝐱,t)⋅(at​𝐱j−𝐱)σt2,wherewj​(𝐱,t)∝exp⁡(−‖𝐱−at​𝐱j‖222​σt2),\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}(\mathbf{x},t)\cdot(a_{t}\,\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x})}{\sigma_{t}^{2}},\quad\text{where}\quad w_{j}(\mathbf{x},t)\propto\exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x}-a_{t}\mathbf{x}_{j}\|^{2}_{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right), (123)

with at=e−t/2a_{t}=e^{-t/2}, σt2=at2​h2+(1−at2)\sigma_{t}^{2}=a_{t}^{2}h^{2}+(1-a_{t}^{2}) and the constant of proportionality chosen to ensure ∑j=1Nwj​(𝐱,t)=1\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}(\mathbf{x},t)=1. This provides a smooth, differentiable score estimate that captures the structure of the training distribution while introducing controlled approximation error.

Recursive training protocol.

We implement the iterative retraining procedure described in Section 1:

  1. 1.

    Generation 0: Sample N=100,000N=100{,}000 points from pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} and construct the initial score estimator s^0\hat{s}_{0}.

  2. 2.

    Generation i→i+1i\to i+1: Form the training mixture qi=α​pdata+(1−α)​p^iq_{i}=\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data}}+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i} by combining ⌊α​N⌋\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor fresh samples from pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} with (N−⌊α​N⌋)(N-\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor) synthetic samples from p^i\hat{p}^{i}.

  3. 3.

    Score update: Construct the new score estimator 𝐬^i+1\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{i+1} from the training mixture qiq_{i}.

  4. 4.

    Sampling: Generate p^i+1\hat{p}^{i+1} by running the reverse diffusion SDE with drift 𝐬^i+1\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{i+1} for 500 Euler-Maruyama steps from T=4T=4 to t0=0.02t_{0}=0.02.

We repeat this process for 20 generations across three fresh data fractions α∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}, with 10 independent runs per configuration to estimate variance.

Divergence estimation.

We estimate the χ2\chi^{2} divergence χ2(p^i∥pdata)\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i}\|p_{\mathrm{data}}) using a binary classifier trained to distinguish samples from p^i\hat{p}^{i} versus pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}. Specifically, we train a 3-layer MLP with SiLU activations for 30 epochs on balanced datasets, then estimate:

χ2(p^i∥pdata)≈𝔼𝐱∼pdata[(p^i​(𝐱)pdata​(𝐱)−1)2]=𝔼𝐱∼pdata[(er^​(𝐱)−1)2],\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i}\|p_{\mathrm{data}})\approx\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\left[\left(\frac{\hat{p}^{i}(\mathbf{x})}{p_{\mathrm{data}}(\mathbf{x})}-1\right)^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\left[(e^{\hat{r}(\mathbf{x})}-1)^{2}\right], (124)

where r^​(𝐱)\hat{r}(\mathbf{x}) is the learned log-density ratio. A similar procedure is used to estimate Ii=χ2(p^i+1∥qi)I_{i}=\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i}) and KL(p^i+1∥qi)\mathrm{KL}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i}).

Score error computation.

For the 10-dimensional Gaussian mixture experiment, the score error 𝐞i​(𝐱,t)=𝐬^θi​(𝐱,t)−𝐬qi⋆​(𝐱,t)\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{x},t)=\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t) is computed as follows. The learned score 𝐬^θi\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{\theta_{i}} is obtained via a soft kernel density estimator (KDE) with bandwidth h=0.6h=0.6 fitted to the training samples from qiq_{i}. The target score 𝐬qi⋆\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}}^{\star} of the mixture qi=α​pdata+(1−α)​p^iq_{i}=\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data}}+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i} is computed analytically using the identity

𝐬qi⋆​(𝐱,t)=α​pdata,t​(𝐱)​𝐬data⋆​(𝐱,t)+(1−α)​p^ti​(𝐱)​𝐬^i​(𝐱,t)α​pdata,t​(𝐱)+(1−α)​p^ti​(𝐱),\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t)=\frac{\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data},t}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{data}}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t)+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\,\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{i}(\mathbf{x},t)}{\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data},t}(\mathbf{x})+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i}_{t}(\mathbf{x})},

where 𝐬data⋆\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{data}}^{\star} is the exact score of the Gaussian mixture (available in closed form), and 𝐬^i\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{i} is the KDE-approximated score of p^i\hat{p}^{i} using 50,00050{,}000 samples from the previous generation.

Score error and score energy.

For each generation ii, we track the score error 𝐞⁡(𝐱,t)\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{x},t) at time t∈[t0,T]t\in[t_{0},T] and for sample 𝐱\mathbf{x} as the difference between the learned model and the true model at this generation given by,

𝐬qi⋆​(𝐱,t)=α​pdata,t​(𝐱)​𝐬data⋆​(𝐱,t)+(1−α)​p^ti​(𝐱)​𝐬^i​(𝐱,t)α​pdata,t​(𝐱)+(1−α)​p^ti​(𝐱).\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t)=\frac{\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data},t}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{data}}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},t)+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\,\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{i}(\mathbf{x},t)}{\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data},t}(\mathbf{x})+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i}_{t}(\mathbf{x})}.

In addition, we track the integrated score error along sampling trajectories:

ε^i2=𝔼⁡[∫0T‖𝐬^i+1​(𝐘^ti,t)−𝐬qi​(𝐘^ti,t)‖22​𝑑t],\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\|\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{i+1}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{t}^{i},t)-\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}}(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{t}^{i},t)\|^{2}_{2}\,dt\right], (125)

For the lower bound, we also compute ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2} taking expectation along trajectories sampled using the target score 𝐬qi\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}}, approximated via the mixture formula.

We estimate, for all generations i∈{0,…,19}i\in\{0,...,19\}, the observability of errors coefficient η^i=Var⁡(𝔼⁡[Mi∣𝐘t0⋆,i])/Var⁡(Mi)\hat{\eta}_{i}=\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[M_{i}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{\star,i}])/\mathrm{Var}(M_{i}), using the following method:
