At each step, we compute the score error 𝐞i​(𝐘s⋆,(j),s)=𝐬^θi​(𝐘s⋆,(j),s)−𝐬qi⋆​(𝐘s⋆,(j),s)\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{\star,(j)},s)=\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{\star,(j)},s)-\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}}^{\star}(\mathbf{Y}_{s}^{\star,(j)},s) and accumulate the discretized martingale:

    Mi(j)≈−∑k=1nsteps𝐞i(𝐘tk⋆,(j),tk)⋅𝐳tk(j)Δ​t,M_{i}^{(j)}\approx-\sum_{k=1}^{n_{\mathrm{steps}}}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{k}}^{\star,(j)},t_{k})\cdot\mathbf{z}_{t_{k}}^{(j)}\sqrt{\Delta t},

    which approximates the Itô integral Mi=−∫t0T𝐞i(𝐘s,s)⋅d𝐁¯sM_{i}=-\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{s},s)\cdot\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{B}}_{s}. The terminal samples 𝐘t0(j)\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{(j)} and martingale values Mi(j)M_{i}^{(j)} are then used to estimate the observability coefficient as described above.

  2. 2.

    Train a regression MLP to predict MiM_{i} from 𝐘t0⋆,i\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{\star,i}.

  3. 3.

    Compute η^i=Var⁡(f^​(𝐘t0⋆,i)/Var⁡(Mi)CLOSE\hat{\eta}_{i}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{f}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{\star,i})/\mathrm{Var}(M_{i}), where f^\hat{f} is the learned regressor.

This provides an empirical estimate of how much score error information is retained in the terminal distribution.

Heatmap for Memory Structure.

To empirically validate the theoretical memory structure in Theorem 4.2, we measure how score errors at each generation propagate to affect the quality of the final distribution. More specifically, to isolate the contribution of generation kk’s score error to DnD_{n}, we run two parallel experiments:

  • •

    Baseline: All generations use their learned scores 𝐬^1,…,𝐬^n\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{n}, yielding divergence DnD_{n} (computed as described above).

  • •

    Ablated at ii: Generation ii uses the true score 𝐬qi\mathbf{s}_{q_{i}} (here chosen to be the well trained (on real data) generation 00 model) instead of 𝐬^i\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{i}, while all other generations use their learned scores, yielding divergence Dn(−i)D_{n}^{(-i)}.

The difference measures how much generation ii’s imperfect score worsened the final distribution:

Contrib⁡[i,n]=Dn−Dn(−i).\mathrm{Contrib}[i,n]=D_{n}-D_{n}^{(-i)}. (126)

The motivation behind this approach is to understand “How much better would p^n\hat{p}^{n} approximate pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} if generation ii had used a perfect score? A large contribution indicates that errors at generation ii significantly degrade the final output, even many generations later.

G.2 Results

Intra-generational bounds.

Figures 3 and 4 validate both Propositions 3.1 and 3.3. The upper bound KL(p^i+1∥qi)≤12ε^i2\mathrm{KL}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i})\leq\frac{1}{2}\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2} holds consistently, with the gap reflecting higher-order terms neglected in the Girsanov analysis. The lower bound χ2(p^i+1∥qi)≥18ηiε⋆,i2\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i+1}\|q_{i})\geq\frac{1}{8}\eta_{i}\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2} is also satisfied, with the tightness depending on the observability structure.

Memory structure.

Figure 5 visualizes the contribution matrix, showing how past score errors propagate to current divergence. The effective memory horizon scales inversely with α\alpha: at α=0.1\alpha=0.1, score errors from 10+ generations ago still contribute significantly, while at α=0.9\alpha=0.9, only the most recent generation matters.

Global error accumulation.

Figure 6 shows the evolution of Di=χ2(p^i∥pdata)D_{i}=\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i}\|p_{\mathrm{data}}) across generations. The empirical trajectories closely follow the theoretical prediction Dn≈∑k=0N−1(1−α)2​(N−1−k)​ε⋆,k2D_{n}\approx\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(1-\alpha)^{2(N-1-k)}\varepsilon_{\star,k}^{2}, confirming the discounted-sum structure of error accumulation. Past generation 44, we can see our control holds, validating our framework.

Observability.

Figure 7 shows that η^i\hat{\eta}_{i} stabilizes to a positive constant after initial transients, with higher α\alpha yielding larger observability. This confirms that score errors on distributions closer to pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} project more strongly onto distinguishable directions, tightening the lower bound. Figure 8 provides qualitative confirmation: at low α\alpha, the learned distribution visibly disperses over generations, while high α\alpha maintains distributional fidelity throughout the recursive process.

G.3 Second Experimental Setup: Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10

Having established the full theoretical framework in the controlled GMM setting, we turn to higher-dimensional image datasets, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 to verify that the core structural predictions hold. extend to high-dimensional image distributions with neural network score estimation.

Focused validation strategy.

In the high-dimensional image setting (d=784d=784), precise estimation of divergences such as χ2(p^i∥pdata)\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i}\|p_{\mathrm{data}}) becomes statistically challenging: density ratio estimation in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality, and classifier-based divergence estimates exhibit high variance. Rather than attempting to verify all theoretical quantities with potentially unreliable estimates, we focus on two robust signatures that remain interpretable at scale:

  1. 1.

    Memory contribution structure. The heatmap visualization of the (1−α)2​(N−k)​ε⋆,k2(1-\alpha)^{2(N-k)}\varepsilon_{\star,k}^{2} contributions in (23) depends only on the structure of error propagation, not on absolute divergence magnitudes. The qualitative pattern— a narrow diagonal band for large α\alpha, and a wide triangular region for small α\alpha—is dimension-independent and directly tests the discounted-sum accumulation formula.

  2. 2.

    Observability coefficient. The ratio ηi=Var⁡(𝔼⁡[Mi∣𝐘t0i,⋆])/Var⁡(Mi)\eta_{i}=\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[M_{i}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}])/\mathrm{Var}(M_{i}) is a normalized quantity in [0,1][0,1] that measures the fraction of score error information retained in terminal samples. Unlike raw divergences, ηi\eta_{i} does not scale with dimension and provides a stable diagnostic across settings.

The memory heatmaps test the structural prediction of Theorem 4.2: that current divergence decomposes as a geometrically-weighted sum of past innovations, with decay rate (1−α)2(1-\alpha)^{2}. If this structure holds empirically, then the theoretical framework captures the essential dynamics of recursive training, even if absolute divergence values are difficult to estimate precisely.

The observability coefficient tests whether our visibility of errors discussion (Section 3.2) remains valid in a fully data-driven experiments: that only gradient-aligned score errors affect the terminal distribution. A stable, non-zero ηi\eta_{i} confirms that our lower bound provides meaningful information in the neural network setting.

Experimental setup.

We train diffusion models on 28×2828\times 28 grayscale images from Fashion-MNIST (N=50,000N=50{,}000 training samples). The score network is a U-Net architecture with:

  • •

    Residual blocks with group normalization and SiLU activations

  • •

    Sinusoidal time embeddings projected through a 2-layer MLP

  • •

    Dropout regularization (p=0.1p=0.1) to prevent overfitting

  • •

    Exponential moving average (EMA) of weights with decay 0.990.99

The ε\varepsilon-prediction objective.

In the standard DDPM formulation (Ho et al., 2020a), the forward diffusion process adds Gaussian noise to a data sample 𝐱0∼pdata\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}} according to a variance schedule {α¯t}t=1T\{\bar{\alpha}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}. The noisy sample at time tt is given by

𝐱t=α¯t​𝐱0+1−α¯t​𝐳,where ​𝐳∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈d).\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{z},\quad\text{where }\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d}).

Here, 𝐳\mathbf{z} is the noise variable—a standard Gaussian vector that represents the stochastic component added during the forward process. The neural network εθ​(𝐱t,t)\varepsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) is trained to predict this noise from the corrupted sample 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, yielding the denoising objective:

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼t∼Unif⁡(t0,T),𝐱0∼pdata,𝐳∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈d)​[‖εθ​(𝐱t,t)−𝐳‖22].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(t_{0},T),\,\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\,\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d})}\Big[\|\varepsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-\mathbf{z}\|^{2}_{2}\Big].

This is equivalent to score matching, since the score of the noisy distribution satisfies ∇𝐱tlogpt(𝐱t)=−𝐳/1−α¯t\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=-\mathbf{z}/\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}, and thus εθ\varepsilon_{\theta} implicitly parameterizes the score function.

Recursive training protocol.

We implement the iterative retraining procedure with fresh data fractions α∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}:

  1. 1.

    Generation 0: Train the base model on real Fashion-MNIST data for 200 epochs with AdamW optimizer (learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}) and cosine learning rate annealing.

  2. 2.

    Generation i→i+1i\to i+1: Construct the training mixture qi=α​pdata+(1−α)​p^iq_{i}=\alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data}}+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{p}^{i} by combining ⌊α​N⌋\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor real images with (1−⌊α​N⌋)(1-\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor) synthetic samples generated via DDPM sampling (Ho et al., 2020a) from the current model.

  3. 3.

    Fine-tuning: Train the new model on qiq_{i} for 100 epochs, with early stopping if validation loss plateaus for 50 epochs.

  4. 4.

    Sampling: Generate synthetic data using 1000-step DDPM sampling with the EMA model weights.

We run 10 generations per α\alpha value, tracking all theoretical quantities throughout the process.

Metric computation.

Computing the quantities from our theoretical framework requires careful adaptation to the high-dimensional image setting.

  • •

    Global divergence Di=χ2(p^i∥pdata)D_{i}=\chi^{2}(\hat{p}^{i}\|p_{\mathrm{data}}): In the CIFAR-10 (resp. Fashion-MNIST) experiments we evaluate distributional drift using a proxy χ2\chi^{2}-divergence computed in a learned feature space rather than pixel space. Concretely, for each generation ii we draw MM synthetic samples 𝐱gen(m)∼p^i\mathbf{x}^{(m)}_{\mathrm{gen}}\sim\hat{p}^{\,i} from the EMA-smoothed DDPM sampler and MM real samples 𝐱real(m)∼pdata\mathbf{x}^{(m)}_{\mathrm{real}}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}} from the CIFAR-10 (resp. Fashion-MNIST) training set (we use M=1000M=1000 in our implementation). We pass images through a fixed auxiliary classifier c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot) trained once on CIFAR-10 (resp. Fashion-MNIST), and extract penultimate-layer embeddings f⁡(𝐱)∈ℝdf(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let {fgen(m)}m=1M\{f^{(m)}_{\mathrm{gen}}\}_{m=1}^{M} and {freal(m)}m=1M\{f^{(m)}_{\mathrm{real}}\}_{m=1}^{M} denote generated and real features. We then fit Gaussian densities in feature space, pf=𝒩⁡(𝝁p,Σp)p_{f}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{p},\Sigma_{p}) using {fgen(m)}\{f^{(m)}_{\mathrm{gen}}\} and qf=𝒩⁡(𝝁q,Σq)q_{f}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{q},\Sigma_{q}) using {freal(m)}\{f^{(m)}_{\mathrm{real}}\}, with empirical mean and covariance (regularized as Σ←Σ+ϵ​I\Sigma\leftarrow\Sigma+\epsilon I for numerical stability, taking a small ϵ\epsilon). The divergence proxy is the Monte Carlo estimate of χ2(pf∥qf)\chi^{2}(p_{f}\|q_{f}) under qfq_{f}:

    χfeat2(p^i∥pdata):=1M∑m=1M(pf​(freal(m))qf​(freal(m))−1)2freal(m)∼qf,\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{feat}}(\hat{p}^{i}\|p_{\mathrm{data}})\;:=\;\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(\frac{p_{f}(f^{(m)}_{\mathrm{real}})}{q_{f}(f^{(m)}_{\mathrm{real}})}-1\right)^{2}\qquad f^{(m)}_{\mathrm{real}}\sim q_{f},

    where the density ratio is evaluated via Gaussian log-likelihoods using a Cholesky factorization of Σp\Sigma_{p} and Σq\Sigma_{q}. This metric captures how far the generated distribution has drifted from the real data distribution along discriminative directions encoded by the classifier features.

  • •

    Score error energy ε^i2\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2} and ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}: We subsample 50 timesteps uniformly from [0,T][0,T] and accumulate ‖εθi+1​(𝐱t,t)−εθi​(𝐱t,t)‖22\|\varepsilon_{\theta_{i+1}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-\varepsilon_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\|^{2}_{2} along sampling trajectories, where εθi​(𝐱t,t)\varepsilon_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) denotes the learned ii-th model according to the ε\varepsilon-prediction mechanism described above. For ε^i2\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}, trajectories are sampled using the new model θi+1\theta_{i+1}; for ε⋆,i2\varepsilon_{\star,i}^{2}, trajectories use the previous model θi\theta_{i}.

  • •

    Observability coefficient ηi\eta_{i}: Exactly as in the 1010-dimensional Gaussian multivariate mixture model, we run paired reverse trajectories using the previous model’s score, recording terminal samples 𝐘t0i,⋆\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star} and the discretized error martingale Mi≈−∑t𝐞i(𝐘t0i,⋆,t)⋅ΔBtM_{i}\approx-\sum_{t}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star},t)\cdot\Delta B_{t}. A regression network is trained to predict MiM_{i} from classifier features of 𝐘t0i,⋆\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}, yielding η^i=Var⁡(f^​(𝐘t0i,⋆))/Var⁡(Mi)\hat{\eta}_{i}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{f}(\mathbf{Y}_{t_{0}}^{i,\star}))/\mathrm{Var}(M_{i}).

Heatmap.

Once again, the procedure here is exactly the same as the one described in the 1010-dimensional Gaussian multivariate mixture model. Theorem 4.2 predicts that score errors propagate with geometric decay:

Contrib⁡[i,n]≈(1−α)2​(N−1−i)​εi2,\mathrm{Contrib}[i,n]\;\approx\;(1-\alpha)^{2(N-1-i)}\varepsilon_{i}^{2}, (127)

where εi2=∫0T‖𝐬^k−𝐬qk‖22​𝑑t\varepsilon_{i}^{2}=\int_{0}^{T}\|\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{k}-\mathbf{s}_{q_{k}}\|^{2}_{2}\,\mathrm{d}t is the path-space score error at generation kk. The factor (1−α)2​(N−1−i)(1-\alpha)^{2(N-1-i)} captures the mitigation induced by fresh data injection: when α\alpha is large, errors decay rapidly; when α\alpha is small, errors persist across many generations. As illustrated in Figure 10 the conclusions of this experiment match the theory, suggesting it also holds in higher dimensions.
